title: Digital safety is shifting from internal product review toward ecosystem-level foresight, early warning, and shared accountability
source_unit: World Economic Forum, Preparing for the Future: The Pillars of Digital Safety Foresight
geography: Organizations and digital ecosystems facing AI, technology, user-behavior, adversarial, regulatory, and dependency changes across sectors and borders

risk_sources.value: AI and other technology advances, user-behaviour shifts, adversarial tactics, regulatory expectations, and broader ecosystem dependencies

safety_boundary.value: internal safety-by-design review is necessary but insufficient

operating_problem.value: organizations need to anticipate conditions that emerge outside their own boundaries

observations.method: The WEF report synthesizes digital-safety practice and foresight into an outward-looking framework for anticipating ecosystem conditions and translating them into organizational preparedness.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies practices and response pathways; it does not estimate the prevalence of digital harms, prove that foresight prevents incidents, or establish a universal governance model.
observations.subgroup: Technology firms, public agencies, platform users, safety teams, regulators, civil society, developers, and communities exposed to digital-system harms.
observations.counterinterpretation: External scanning can improve preparedness while also expanding surveillance, compliance burden, or corporate discretion over contested social risks.

pillars.value: frame and govern; sense; model; assess readiness; install early warning; synthesize

sequence.value: from defining the risk frame through sensing, modelling, readiness assessment, warning, and synthesis

governance_link.value: foresight is intended to connect external change detection with organizational decision-making

observations.method: The publication organizes foresight into six repeatable pillars rather than treating risk scanning as a one-time horizon exercise.
observations.uncertainty: The pillars are a design framework; the report does not provide comparative evidence that each pillar has equal value or that organizations can implement them with similar resources.
observations.subgroup: Safety and risk leaders, product teams, policy and legal functions, intelligence and trust-and-safety teams, boards, regulators, and affected users.
observations.counterinterpretation: A formal foresight sequence can produce documentation without changing incentives, product decisions, resource allocation, or user protection.

denominator.unit: response pathways presented by the framework

response_pathways.value: four response pathways for translating foresight into practical action

response_goal.value: strengthen preparedness, resilience, and coordination in a rapidly changing digital environment

coordination_scope.value: internal teams and the wider ecosystem of users, adversaries, regulators, technologies, and dependencies

observations.method: The report pairs the six foresight pillars with four response pathways designed to move from anticipation to organizational action.
observations.uncertainty: The pathways are not a measured intervention effect, implementation inventory, or guarantee that coordination resolves conflicts among safety, access, innovation, privacy, and commercial incentives.
observations.subgroup: Organizations deploying AI and digital products, public institutions, supply-chain partners, safety researchers, users, and communities with limited ability to exit harmful systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coordination can improve resilience but may centralize control, create interoperability dependence, or shift liability without giving affected users meaningful voice or remedy.

shared_responsibility.value: digital safety requires a broader ecosystem approach rather than isolated organizational review

trust_condition.value: resilience depends on anticipating change and coordinating across sectors and borders

user_implication.value: user behaviour and user-facing harms are part of the external conditions that shape digital safety

observations.method: The report connects foresight, preparedness, resilience, and coordination to the changing relationship between digital products, users, institutions, and adversaries.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not measure trust, user harm, remedy access, or distributional outcomes, and it leaves implementation and accountability arrangements context-dependent.
observations.subgroup: Users, vulnerable populations, public-interest organizations, firms, regulators, and cross-border institutions responsible for digital safety and accountability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Calling safety a shared responsibility can diffuse accountability unless specific actors retain duties to prevent harm, disclose risks, and provide correction and remedy.

related_sources.claim: Related WEF cyber-risk context on AI, geopolitics, cyber inequity, and systemic dependence.

boundary: This record adds a digital-safety foresight and ecosystem-governance route linking external risk sensing, AI and user-behavior change, adversarial tactics, regulation, early warning, preparedness, coordination, trust, and accountability. It is a practice framework, not a cyber-incident census, respondent-level harm data, causal evaluation, implementation audit, or proof that shared responsibility produces remedy or equitable safety.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official WEF publication page was reviewed for the external risk-source framing, six foresight pillars, four response pathways, and ecosystem-level preparedness and coordination claims; the related cyber outlook was used only as contextual linkage.
